Visual Perception Failure.Object / Attribute Misrecognition: The model misidentifies visible entities or their basic properties (category, color, size, count, pose) despite them being clearly depicted. Examples: calling a kitchen a living room (Case 1), saying a rabbit is looking for food instead of bringing back a visible baby rabbit (Case 22), miscounting how many toy eggs or circles are opened/cut when each action is shown (Cases 31, 35).
Visual Perception Failure.Spatial / Temporal Relation Misperceptio: The model sees the right objects but fails to track where or when they are, leading to wrong answers about positions, heights, order, or persistence. Examples: mislocating the camera relative to characters in a car (Cases 4, 10), confusing which dog is upstairs vs downstairs (Case 23), misjudging which position is highest (monkey on bus vs tree, Cases 19–20; person on pole vs rope, Case 11), or miscounting how many people are present despite all appearing on screen (Case 37).
Visual Perception Failure.Action / Event Misperception: The model misreads what concrete actions occur, even though they are visually explicit. Examples: claiming no mech pilot uses a bat when one clearly does and self‑destructs (Case 6), saying a woman doesn’t rescue a man when she visibly cuts him free right after defeating the enemy (Case 8), or saying a gunman gets off the car instead of shooting between phone uses (Case 14).
Visual Perception Failure.Object Presence / State Tracking Error: The model fails to track which items are present, added, removed, or where they are stored over time. Examples: wrong counts of items in a box or backpack before/after specific insertions/removals (Cases 39, 42), wrong number of pens remaining on a table after placing a spoon (Case 40), or misjudging whether the number of objects on a desk has changed (Case 30).
Visual Perception Failure.Text / Symbol / Fine-detail Misreading: The model misinterprets visually available symbolic or fine-grained cues (text, small UI elements, timing markers) that are needed for the answer. Examples: misreading which lever operations correspond to orbit switches (Case 21), or mis-estimating scene durations when timestamps and cuts clearly indicate the total (Case 5).

Reasoning or Hallucination Failure.Counterfactual or Instruction-Ignoring R: The model ignores explicit hypothetical conditions or task constraints and instead answers about the literal scene or drifts off-task. Examples: the bullet-count question assumes an initial 10 bullets and asks for a remaining count, but the model insists no option fits instead of applying the described firing sequence (Case 36); questions asking for step-by-step solutions are answered with narrative that never actually computes the requested quantity (e.g., Case 3).
Reasoning or Hallucination Failure.Causal / Temporal Logic Error: The model sees the right events but draws the wrong causal or temporal conclusions. Examples: the black man doesn’t rescue the woman because a second explosion blocks him (Case 2), but the model invents another rescuer; the second fight clearly occurs in the kitchen after the living room fight, but the model concludes it is again in the living room (Case 1); or mis-ordering who shoots next in a repeated archery sequence (Case 38).
Reasoning or Hallucination Failure.Role / Intent / Relationship Misinterpre: The model misinfers characters’ roles, relationships, or intentions from the same visual evidence. Examples: men in suits watching a firefight on TV are masterminds, not random special forces or passersby (Case 18); two attackers of the same motorcyclist are on the same side, not opposed (Case 9); the monkey is trying to drive pigeons away with a scare device, not befriend them (Case 24); a big rabbit leaves the cage to retrieve a missing baby, not to forage (Case 22).
Reasoning or Hallucination Failure.Hallucinated Narrative or Details: The model fabricates long, coherent but unsupported stories or entities not present in the video. Examples: inventing a full battle sequence with ejection and parachute when the pilot actually crash-lands and fights on the ground (Case 7); describing a mech battle with no baseball bat (Case 6); or claiming a rabbit gains a new flamethrower-like weapon instead of being helped by another rabbit (Case 29).
Reasoning or Hallucination Failure.Counting / Aggregation Reasoning Error: The model observes individual events but fails to aggregate them correctly into totals or comparisons, even when each step is visible. Examples: miscounting how many rooms George visits (Case 25), how many orbit switches occur (Case 21), how many times a shooter’s position changes (Case 15), or how many people are sitting on the ground vs total in frame (Case 34).
